subject: Climate & Environment
title: The 30 by 30 Target
description: A quick, practical guide to The 30 by 30 Target.

hook.text: In 2022, 196 nations agreed to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean by 2030.

buildup.text: Currently about 17% of land and 8% of ocean are under some form of protection.

discovery.text: Meeting the target would double marine protection and significantly expand land reserves.

twist.text: Protection on paper means little without enforcement, funding, and community involvement.

climax.text: Indigenous-led conservation has the best track record — it must be central to the plan.

punchline.text: Thirty percent is a start. Nature needs room to breathe.

quiz.question: What does the '30 by 30' target aim to protect by 2030?

details.summary: The 30 by 30 target, adopted at COP15 in 2022, commits nations to protect 30 percent of land and ocean by 2030. Currently only about 17 percent of land and 8 percent of ocean are formally protected, meaning the goal requires roughly doubling marine protection in under a decade.
details.whyItMatters: 30 by 30 is the most ambitious global biodiversity target ever agreed. Its success depends on funding, indigenous rights, and political will to protect genuinely critical areas.
takeaways: Currently about 17 percent of land is formally protected
Only about 8 percent of ocean is in marine protected areas
The target was adopted by 196 countries at COP15 in Montreal

faq.question: Is 30 percent enough to stop biodiversity loss?
faq.answer: Many scientists argue that 50 percent or more of Earth needs protection to halt the extinction crisis. However, 30 by 30 is seen as a politically achievable milestone that would significantly improve current protection levels if implemented effectively.

faq.question: How will 30 by 30 affect indigenous communities?
faq.answer: Indigenous peoples manage an estimated 36 percent of remaining intact ecosystems. The target recognizes indigenous rights and traditional stewardship, but past protected-area designations have forcibly displaced communities, making equitable implementation critical.
